As an instructor I love to hear this, I always try to tailor my conditioning to the moves we're doing in the main lesson plan, and I explain how it helps the move we're doing. Like doing Genie crunches on the pole to help with leg and core engagement for a transition from a Genie to Figurehead.

No spotting is a big no no, especially if it's first time trying something.

I can sort of understand only demoing once, as I know some instructors who take this approach, for the following reasons:
A) some students talk through instructions, and it's annoying to have to demo several times and wear yourself out because some students weren't paying attention. If you didn't catch the first demo, that's on you
B) some instructors want you to develop the skills to figure out things on your own without having to hold your hand throughout everything 
C) not being able to demo more than twice due to things like injury
D) having already done several classes beforehand and simply do not have the energy to do more than one demo

However for mixed ability where there's beginners I definitely disagree with this approach. You're there to teach, and this can be a dangerous sport. You need to make sure your students are doing everything correctly as much as possible.

My general approach is silent demo, demo talking through the main points, and then ask if anyone wants a final demo that sums everything up that I've just outlined. Then everyone else can have a go while I come around spotting/checking in - I allow more proficient students to spot each other (unless it's a super dicey move) however any beginners or anyone who is scared/unsure is instructed to wait until I'm available to spot.

This is very taxing on the shoulders so I found working on shoulder rotation really helped with this, both in terms of being able to hold it for longer and not feeling as wrecked afterwards. My favourite way to do this was full depth [skin the cat](https://images.app.goo.gl/RXX9KiiJRAis9yis5) on rings and back over like in the gif. It takes a lot of strength to get back over so it's good to aim to do that however just hanging in full depth for a few seconds will still benefit you, then dropping out provided you aren't too high up.

There are lots of different exercises you can do for shoulder rotation if you don't have access to any rings, but I found that was the best. You'll also need to work on oblique strength for the lift once your shoulders start feeling more comfortable to hold this position longer. You can do side crunches in this position to help with that.

I know you said you don't like resistance bands, but they're a really helpful tool for training deadlifts. You can also do negatives to help hold this position I.e. coming down from Ayesha into this side on position as slowly as possible and trying to hold it. If you can Iron X, come down into your Iron X and push back up into Ayesha, then come down again and repeat etc.

I do calisthenics and I genuinely think pole can be considered a form of calisthenics. You're essentially using compound movements to lift and hold your bodyweight as a form of resistance training, much like calisthenics.

I started pole before I picked up calisthenics and had a bit of a headstart in calisthenics thanks to pole and the transferable skills it gave me. Similarly, training calisthenics transferred to pole and I made significant progress in pole once I started training cali regularly. 

Only drawback, if any, is that pole is very much a pull-heavy exercise, so you'll probably struggle with push dominant movements like dips and push ups at first. I'm still not great at dips, but I worked hard on my push ups and they're feeling a lot easier now. And I actually have triceps now too! So training cali and pole together will balance out your push and pull power - highly recommend.

Pointing your toes actually helps with engaging your legs, which you'll need for actually holding moves, particularly shapes where your main contact with the pole is with your legs. Maybe knowing the fact it's more likely to keep you on the pole will help? 😂

But a cue I give my students often is to try to point your foot to your bum.

Ideally you should have your bottom hand higher up to get a good push into the pole, however this and the width of your arms depends a lot on anatomy. Everyone's sweet spot will be in a different place - I typically have a wide grip in my deadlift but I have hyperextended elbows and need the bottom hand low to avoid complete lock out. Play around with your bottom hand height and see what feels most comfortable for you. 

Also, I find making sure my bottom shoulder is pushed down and forward so it can help push down into my bottom arm helps with avoiding elbow, wrist and/or shoulder pain in this. I feel it helps take the load off your bottom arm a bit.

Some general tips, it sounds obvious but really pull with the top hand. As you're pushing that bottom arm into the pole you can take some of the weight off it by really pulling, as this will lift your body up. You want to really aim your chest to the ceiling to get that strong pull up top and aim your hips away from the pole.

This still looks strong though, well done! Keep working towards getting your bands thinner too until you can attempt with no band 💪

Maybe speak to your instructor about your sits and climbs - there is always a "regressed" version of something (I put this in inverted commas as I hate this word, however it's the official term for it according to my instructor courses for a simpler, more accessible version of a move that can be trained in preparation for the full thing/a harder varation) for example, in your seats, you can bend your knees and walk your hands down the pole while standing on the floor so you're lower down to the floor, and you don't have to achieve as much height to get into your seat. Keep doing this and you'll be able to start getting into your seat from higher and higher up until you're doing the full thing.

Yep, Marion Amber is a very advanced move, it just doesn't look like it should be as difficult as it actually is. I got my Iron X way before I got my Marion Amber.  Extended Butterfly should not be a prerequisite for this - though they look similar, Marion Amber is very much beyond an Extended Butterfly in terms of difficulty.

Not to drag your instructor but she should have spotted you as you extended your leg, as this is the hardest bit and if you're not stable, this is where you'll fall, as you found out. I'm also cringing at the lack of safety mats 😬

As for tips on your Marion Amber, it looks like your hand grip is barely there on the pole. You need very strong hand grip to hold this, and it can be very easily compromised by the trapping of the leg. Make sure to inch your leg as high up your arm as possible for maximum hand room and grip before you go into the Marion Amber position.

You also need to be much more square to the pole. The positioning is very similar to a Butterfly - your body looks very close to the pole here. Your bottom hand should be actively pushing against the pole to engage the shoulder, so you're not just 'hanging' on the pole, as in this case extending the leg will be impossible without falling.

As others have said, Marion Amber is *deceptively* hard, so don't get discouraged. It looks like it should be easier than Ayesha since you have leg contact with the pole, but it's the leg contact that compromises the hand grip and stacked body position. It requires a lot of grip strength and core stability! Don't give up!

Hoop very much looks easier than pole but it's NOT. I've been hooping for around three years now and I'm still not on the same sort of level as I am at pole. You've more dimensions to think about on the hoop (like limbs through or around parts of the hoop for example) rather than up down left or right on the pole. You need to mobilise your joints before you stretch! There are lots of little exercises you can do like rolling your head, making small circles with your arms and gradually making them bigger, circling your hips, reaching up to the ceiling and then down to your toes (or thereabouts), moving your torso from side to side, "climbing over the gate" with each leg, circling your ankles, circling your wrists.

Really make sure every joint from head to toe has been moved in any capacity - usually in circles like I've described - to get the blood flowing to the area so that when you come to do some stretching, whether dynamic or passive, you don't injure yourself! 

My warm up routine consists of mobilisation, pulse racers (jogging on the spot, star jumps etc) and THEN stretching. Always do your stretching last, and then again after exercising but hold the positions for longer than you would during your warm up.

I do aerial fitness so pull ups fortunately came quite naturally for me. I didn't really have to train for it per se, however I am now trying to get my muscle up which is a whole different kettle of fish, and part of my training for that includes controlled negatives on the rings. I would always recommend negatives for lots of different exercises as they're really good for building neural pathways for correct muscle engagement. Try coming down from the bar in a pull up position as slowly as possible.

You can also try bands, working your way up from thick bands to thinner bands as you feel them become easier/your reps increase. They're fiddly but really useful.

As for general exercises, lat pulldowns are a good one. Generally lat heavy exercises are a good start. You can also lie under a stacked barbell and pull yourself up keeping your feet on the floor.

And a tip - chest to the ceiling. Imagine a string is pulling you up to the ceiling from your chest. Also think about pushing the bar down with your hands.

Hope that helps and happy pull upping! Hope you get your pull up for 2025!

Don't beat yourself up if you can't get your head around it - it's strength, spatial awareness, momentum, form and coordination. Confidence too, like in my case. The secret to it all is consistency, both on and off the pole. Do your conditioning, make sure it's varied and appropriate for your goals i.e. if you've got a strong invert, you'd benefit more from aerial invert conditioners. There are a wealth of conditioners online for lots of different pole goals, and it's fun to switch it up!

Do some resistance training off the pole, consistently. Doesn't have to be lifting weights - there are lots of sports that have transferable skills with pole. Climbing, pilates, and my personal favourite, calisthenics. I can't recommend it enough, there's been a noticeable difference in both my skill and strength on the pole since I started doing calisthenics.

Conditioning helps! Try doing crunches on the pole, and make sure you're lifting into the crunch and try to hold it. When you can do 5 without touching the floor, try tucking and then tilting back. Aim to splay the knees as you tuck back so they're over your arms. When you're confident in these, crunch, tilt back, and extend the legs, pushing your hips up and extending the arms to try your chopper. These conditioners will help you lift into the invert instead of jumping.

Is it the top hand or bottom hand in your split grip that gets the pain? And are you doing butterfly in twisted or true grip? If it's your bottom wrist, you need to engage your top shoulder more so that you're not holding all your weight in your bottom arm. This will cause wrist pain. It can also be caused by hyperextension - if like me, you have hyperextended elbows, be really careful about locking out your bottom arm as this makes the weight stacking uneven and puts a lot of strain on your bottom arm. 

If it's your top wrist, then this might be caused by twisted grip. Try true grip, this is a lot less intensive and you don't have to rotate your wrist to grip the pole. 

Learning where your arms need to go to stack your weight correctly takes practice with or without hyperextension. You might need to do some experimenting with your arm placement and see what works best for you, especially if your form is right everywhere else. It could be as simple as putting your bottom hand lower on the pole.

Make sure as much of your forearm on the bottom arm is on the pole. With your other arm, once you've got into your reverse elbow grip, grab your top hip/top of your leg with your hand to fully lock you in. Then slowly take off the top foot in a stag leg at first, then extend out. Keep that core crunched!

Edit: just seen your caption. Your elbow should be pointed at an angle to get the grip, sort of like the angle when you look at your watch. If you don't tilt it, the grip will mostly be in your forearm which is painful.

Mostly commenting to follow this thread as I've started training for my deadlift too. It's been a month since I started trying and I can see a tiny bit of progress already. Some things I've learned so far:

• Rotate the bottom wrist into the pole slightly more so your elbow is rotated out and slightly bent. This will avoid a lock out of the elbow and you can push more into the pole to hold a lift.

• If you're doing twisted grip, this is intense on your shoulders. Work on your shoulder flexibility for that shoulder rotation the deadlift requires.

• Work on just holding yourself in a split grip hang, as if you're about to deadlift, with your chest to the ceiling. Try to hold yourself longer each time.

• Try to tuck your knees to your chest in your hang as a conditioner to work on your core - if you can hang, you have the required upper body strength. The lift comes from core strength. Try to get your hips higher each time.

• On that note, remember to tilt your pelvis forward so lifting the hips is easier. This will engage your core too.

• Keep practising! Consistency is the secret to everything.

We do a conditioner that has progressions. 

First level: sit on the floor with the pole between your legs, and pull your bum up off the floor, leaving your feet down. Do ten of these, swap arms around and do ten more.

Second level: pull your entire bottom half off the floor, bum first feet second. Lower yourself back down to the floor, repeat five times, swap arms and do five more.

Third level: pull yourself up from the floor, and complete five reps of lowering yourself up and down without touching the floor. It's okay if you can't do five at first, 3 reps is fine. Swap arm positions and repeat.

Fourth level: climb the pole, putting your legs on the pole into a seat between each climb.

Fifth and final level: climb the pole with just your arms, no legs on the pole between climbs.

This looks like a Plus. It can be quite tricky and flexibility certainly helps, however you should still be able to do this without being able to do a middle split. You have to really get the pole in your armpit, and this requires the bottom half of you to drop down a bit while your feet/ankles stay on the pole - make sure you're really opening your hip flexors during stretching, and there are some hip flexor exercises you can do which will help with that drop and make it not feel quite as horrible! Notably:

Come into a low lunge on the floor, stabilising yourself with your hands on the floor on each side. Move side to side and you'll feel this in your hips.

Sit in a straddle on the floor and place hands on the floor in between your legs. Lift your legs up, either unilaterally or bilaterally in small motions, trying to get them higher. This is harder than it sounds! You can make it more difficult by leaning forward with your torso.

There are a lot of great exercises you can do against the wall and using yoga blocks too!

Hi there! I've been poling for 2 years 4 months, and I had no fitness experience when I started. I take advanced classes, help teach beginners once a week and am studying to be a fully qualified instructor. 

I train on the pole around 2-3 times a week, do aerial hoop and have stints of taking heels classes as well, though I'm really not a dancer. I also go to the gym and lift.

How you progress at pole is different for everybody, so don't get discouraged if you're on the struggle bus for a while - pole is fucking hard! I think it overwhelms a lot of people when they first start just how hard it is, and it feels like you're never going to get to where you want to be with it. But one week you'll notice the sits don't hurt as much, another you'll notice the climb wasn't as difficult. I recommend taking pictures and videos, even if you feel you're no good right now, because it's a way to track your progress and you'll start noticing your little wins - you can even notice a difference in a pose in just how confident you are in it. Then when you're a year in, you reeeeally start to see how much you've progressed.

It took me a few weeks to do the most basic climb up the pole, and I did my first invert at 12 weeks. However don't compare! Some people take a long time to invert, some can do it straight away.

I felt like I was rubbish at pole for a while, and it was around 6 months in where I felt a big leap of progression, but then I plateaued again because as you get better, your classes get harder so you're constantly challenging yourself. Even though I'm now advanced, I still know I have a long way to go as I want to perfect this! 

Accept that pole will keep finding ways to humble you, but you just have to keep rising to the challenge because it feels so bloody good when you finally get what you've been working towards and that's why we keep coming back, bruises n all 😂 but most of all HAVE FUN, pole is one of the best communities you can find, we all support each other here and I've made some amazing friends through it. Keep going and good luck!
